papers.title: Eliminating Make-Whole Uplifts with a Minimum-Cost Uniform Price Adder
papers.abstract: Co-optimizing energy and flexible ramping reserves may dispatch generators at locational marginal prices (LMPs) below their submitted energy offer prices, necessitating out-of-market make-whole payments. Such payments create discriminatory settlements among generators and may incentivize strategic bidding for higher profits. This paper proposes LMP+U, an in-market uniform price adder to LMP for transmission-constrained networks, which minimizes demand payments subject to zero out-of-market make-whole uplift, preserves LMP-based congestion charges, and provides locally truthful bidding incentives for price-taking generators. We also identify conditions under which a price-taking generator can increase its profit by inflating its energy offer under conventional LMP with make-whole uplift. Numerical simulations illustrate the properties of LMP+U and its advantages over conventional LMP in congested networks.

papers.title: Exchange rights and vacancy priorities
papers.abstract: Many institutions let incumbents exchange positions while allocating announced vacancies by priority, withdrawing positions released by vacancy recipients. A policy specifies permitted exchanges, vacancy eligibility, and priorities. A strategy-proof, individually rational rule protecting exchange rights and vacancy priorities exists precisely for policies without conflict cycles. Restricting protection to first choices does not enlarge this class. We introduce the propose-and-trade rule, which satisfies these properties and selects the applicant-optimal core allocation under every conflict-free policy. We identify when propose-and-trade is the unique strategy-proof, individually rational rule protecting first choices. These axioms characterize deferred acceptance and top trading cycles in their classic settings. Under a policy with a conflict cycle, propose-and-trade is manipulable but protects exchange rights and first-choice claims. Replacing it with any strategy-proof rule makes some applicant worse off at some profile. We show when priority reform alone can eliminate conflict cycles and when eligibility or exchange permissions must change.

papers.title: Partially Identified Ambiguity
papers.abstract: This paper addresses the normative question of whether one should condition on the data when performing robust Bayesian analysis under partial identification. We provide an ex ante representation of the conditional Gamma-minimax criterion and show that it can violate Aumann plausibility, a set-valued generalization of the rational expectations property. Our main characterization result establishes that Aumann plausibility holds if and only if the decision maker's prior set exhibits partially identified ambiguity. The latter condition requires the prior set to equal the Aumann expectation of a random set of distributions supported on the parameter's identified sets. We interpret these results as suggesting that conditional Gamma-minimax should only be used under partially identified ambiguity. The implications for various robust Bayesian methods are discussed.

papers.title: Normative Ceilings and Stochastic Giving
papers.abstract: People randomize when they allocate money to others, and what else is available changes how they randomize: adding an alternative can raise the probability that an existing one is chosen, in violation of Regularity. We characterize a model of stochastic choice in which a selfish decision maker faces norm-driven social pressure and the menu matters only through one scalar, the normative ceiling, defined as the most pro-social alternative available. We introduce two conditions on cross-menu comparisons: comparisons line up through a single rescaling attached to each menu's most normative alternative, and higher normative levels are more selective. Together with standard positivity, continuity, acyclicity, order and richness requirements, these conditions force the randomization cost to depend on the menu only through the ceiling. Raising the ceiling makes the cost uniformly more curved. Random utility and baseline perturbed utility models imply Regularity; models of deliberate randomization necessarily violate it; ours does neither. Instead, our model predicts that Regularity can fail only when the ceiling rises across behaviorally distinguishable levels, and that it then fails at the least selfish alternatives. This prediction is a sign restriction with no free parameters, and we show how nested menus test it.

papers.title: Rethinking Arrow--Debreu: A New Framework for Exchange
papers.abstract: This paper revisits the Arrow--Debreu general equilibrium framework through the lens of effective trade, emphasizing the distinction between theoretical and realizable market interactions. We develop the Effective Trade Model (ETM), where transactions arise from bilateral feasibility rather than aggregate supply and demand desires. Within this framework, we establish the main properties of the price-demand correspondence and prove the existence of Nash equilibria, incorporating production, money, and network topology. Our results show that equilibrium is shaped by transaction constraints, subjective pricing, and decentralized negotiation, rather than by universal market-clearing conditions, and thereby call into question the foundations of welfare theory.

papers.title: Bayesian Persuasion without Commitment
papers.abstract: We introduce a model of persuasion in which a sender without any commitment power privately gathers information about an unknown state of the world and then chooses what to verifiably disclose to a receiver. The receiver does not know how many experiments the sender is able to run, and may therefore be uncertain as to whether the sender disclosed all of her information. Despite this challenge, we show that, under general conditions, the sender is able to achieve the same payoff as in the full-commitment Bayesian persuasion case.
